description: We are ALLPA, a team formed by graduates from UDEP, UNP and UTEC.
summary:
SURCO is a web app that gives smallholder farmers in Piura, Peru, a crop-rotation plan that is provably optimal. Most tools stop at showing NASA data on a map; SURCO turns that data into a concrete planting decision. The farmer draws their parcel and answers six simple steps. SURCO then combines NASA observations for that exact field (NASA POWER climate, HLS vegetation health, NASADEM slope) with official ANA water rights, regional crop statistics, and El Niño probabilities from ENFEN. We chose these datasets deliberately and rejected SMAP and GRACE, because their resolution is coarser than the valley itself.

An optimization engine, cross-checked by a second independent method, searches every possible multi-season plan and guarantees no better plan exists within the farmer's water and land limits. It returns three strategies (more income, less water, better soil), each stress-tested across El Niño, La Niña and neutral years, rated for risk, and explained in plain language. Plans export as a one-page PDF or Excel sheet.

This matters because water is scarce in Piura, El Niño shocks keep coming back, and one wrong crop can cost a whole season.

Video of 3 minutes: https://youtu.be/UPxbnU8q10s
Live demo: https://surco-v1.onrender.com/
details:
What it does and how it works

SURCO turns NASA Earth observations into a crop-rotation plan for a single farm. In a 6-step wizard, the farmer draws their parcel on a map, picks their current crops, enters their water allotment and, optionally, any permanent crops such as lemon or banana. SURCO then automatically retrieves data for that exact field:

NASA POWER for temperature, rainfall, extreme-rain days and frost risk

HLS satellite imagery for vegetation health (NDVI), with MODIS as a fallback

NASADEM for slope

It combines these with official ANA water allotments, crop statistics from the Piura Regional Agriculture Directorate (DRA Piura), and El Niño, La Niña and neutral scenarios weighted by ENFEN's official probabilities.

A mixed-integer optimization engine then builds a plan across several seasons. It respects water and land limits, multi-season crops, and rotation effects on the soil, and it guarantees that the plan is optimal. A second, independent method (dynamic programming) reaches the same optimum, which confirms the result. SURCO returns three strategies: more income, less water and better soil. Each one comes with a robustness rating (Very safe, Safe or Risky) and a plain-language explanation.

Benefits

Clear answers: farmers get a concrete, justified answer to "what should I plant next season?" instead of raw maps.

Realistic limits: plans respect the farmer's actual water rights. For example, SURCO flags honestly that rice doesn't fit the allotment.

Climate risk made visible: risk is shown before planting, not after a bad El Niño year.

Ready for the field: plans export to a one-page PDF or an Excel sheet.

Works offline from AI: an optional assistant can explain results, but the app works fully without it.

Intended impact

Smallholders in the Chira and Piura valleys face scarce water and recurring El Niño shocks, so one wrong crop can cost a whole season. SURCO aims to cut that risk, save water and protect soil health. Extension agents and cooperatives can also use it to advise many farmers at once.

Tools and technologies

Code: Python with FastAPI and Jinja, plus JavaScript with Leaflet for the map.

Data storage: SQLite with SQLModel and Alembic.

Optimization: the CBC solver.

Data access: NASA POWER API, Microsoft Planetary Computer (HLS), MODIS, NASADEM.

Optional assistant: swappable between a rule-based mode, Ollama, and any OpenAI-compatible service.

Testing and docs: 152 automated tests with pytest and Playwright, and a 39-page technical manual in LaTeX.

Deployment: Docker on Render's free tier. No special hardware is needed; it runs in a browser.

Creativity

Decisions, not dashboards: SURCO turns satellite data into a mathematically optimal decision.

Explained in farmer language: results come in plain words, with the math available in a technical mode.

Grounded in real limits: water rights and official El Niño forecasts drive the optimization.

Factors we considered

Data resolution: we rejected SMAP (9 km) and GRACE (about 330 km) because they are coarser than the 7–13 km valley.

Real, sourced data only: 53 cited sources, and only crops actually grown in Piura.

Simplicity for farmers: 6 steps, 3 options and a single disclaimer.

Transparency: every number can be traced to its source.

Zero cost: free data and free hosting.

Honesty: the app shows its limits instead of hiding infeasible results.
